topics.title: [grug] Compute the MoE routing-weight gradient on the expert side
topics.body:
The hero takes its MoE routing-weight gradient from the expert MLP's own backward, so the backward needs neither the expert outputs nor their return transport, and the hero saves the routed output instead of recomputing the expert down projection, the return all-to-all and the combine. The step shortens by 3.14% (13.542 to 13.130 s). Peak HBM rises by ~20 GiB to ~125 GiB of the 143.75 GiB pool.

`moe_mlp` and `MoEExpertMlp` gain `routing_weight_gradient`. The default, `EXACT`, keeps the expert outputs and differentiates the combine, as before. `EXPERT_SIDE` is the new path, which the hero selects; other implementations reject it. Where w * dout rounds to zero in the cotangent dtype (a zero weight, or in float16 a normal weight times a small cotangent), its gradient is zero or inexact. The hero's routing weights are positive renormalized sigmoids and its cotangents bf16, which has fp32's exponent range. Forward, dx, dW13 and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; the routing-weight gradient differs at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp) at nonzero weights.

The gradient with respect to the combine weight w[t,k] is dS[t,k] = <dout[t], y[t,k]>, the only backward consumer of the expert down projection's output y. Since dy = w * dout and dh = dy W2^T, the same value is rowsum(dh * h) / w, built from tensors the expert MLP backward already holds. One custom VJP from dispatch to combine returns s = <h, dh> per expert row, sends it back with one [C, 1] f32 all-to-all per chunk, and forms dS = s / w in f32; dropped and padded slots get 0 by selection. The portable `ragged_dot` expert MLP, used without QuACK, still keeps its outputs for the row dot. The backward's transports reuse the forward transfers' offsets, swapped, and on GPU its weighted output cotangents come from #9832's scatter kernel.

The saved routed output needs a larger remat budget, so the carry offload defaults to a 0.78 memory fraction and an XLA memory-limit slop factor of 105 (114 GiB, against 87.7 GiB at 0.75 and 85, below the backward's ~105 GiB). With the backward's transports no longer ordered after the recompute's, several collectives in flight gave run-to-run different gradients or hung on GB200, so every ragged run forces a collective overlap limit of 1.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: Skip S3 directory creation in StoragePath
topics.body:
Make `StoragePath.mkdirs()` a no-op for S3 paths. FineStore eval archives already use this Rigging API, so FineStore needs no S3-specific check. Other filesystems keep their existing behavior.

S3 prefixes need no directory creation. If both `head_bucket` and `get_bucket_location` fail, s3fs treats the bucket as absent. Directory creation then attempts `CreateBucket` and can report `InvalidRegion`, hiding the original check errors.

Related issues:

- [Antidoom eval archive failure](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/616): FineStore directory creation reached `CreateBucket` and failed with `InvalidRegion`.
- [SkyRL checkpoint upload failure #9213](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9213): s3fs directory creation reached the same error during training.
- [Compiler-cache recovery #9202](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9202): rclone required `--s3-no-check-bucket` to avoid `InvalidRegion`.

topics.title: [grug] Add remat, pooled-wave and collective benchmarks for June on AMD
topics.body:
Add the flags and scripts used for the June Snowball MI350X measurements in #9812.

The synthetic benchmark supports `--remat-mode {recompute_all,save_moe}`. At batch 8, `save_moe` reduced step time from 0.716 s to 0.610 s while using 10 GiB more memory ([results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6025360841), jobs 453346-453411). `--watch-interval N` sets the gradient watch interval; 0 turns off the watch step. Turning it off reduced batch 8 peak memory from 164.3 to 150.2 GiB. The batch 8-64 sweep used this setting ([results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6026123091), jobs 453351-453384).

The benchmark also accepts `--capacity-factor`, `--pooled-transport-capacity-factor`, and `--num-expert-waves` to run `--moe-impl fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all`. The June `GrugModelConfig` passes the latter two settings to the Grug MoE layer. At batch 64 with 1 wave, pooled-wave took 2.459 s per step versus 2.427 s for ring ([results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027494656), jobs 453584, 453635, 453658).

`run_gpu.sh` wraps Slurm runs on the AMD HPC Fund cluster. It disables XLA command buffers, which caused NaN gradients and segfaults after a few steps on this ROCm stack, and filters ROCm log noise.

`experiments/amd_collective_ceiling/jax_collectives.py` measures all-gather, reduce-scatter, all-reduce, and all-to-all bus bandwidth under `shard_map` on one node, optionally alongside a matmul. On 8x MI350X, all-gather reached 392 GB/s for the 1.34 GB EP message, matching rccl-tests ([results](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027494656), jobs 453572, 453633, 453651). It sits beside `experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling` from #9840; the two could later share one directory.

Commits after the GPU runs have not been rerun on GPU. They restrict `--ops` to known collectives, pass the timing settings as a dataclass, make the warmup run at least one call, and reject an invalid pooled-wave setup before the model state is built.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [eval] Run each evaluation as a StepSpec
topics.body:
Run each selected evaluation as its own StepSpec. StepRunner owns locking, retries, and success caching at each result path. An Iris restart skips successful steps before starting their model servers. Each step starts its candidate and optional judge server; `--max-concurrent` bounds simultaneous evaluations (default 8). A server startup failure writes a failed record only for the affected evaluation.

The eval launcher binds StepSpecs when it submits a prepared batch, after caller changes to priority or executor. Each submission gets fresh run IDs, including AIME repeats. Step identities include the resolved model and evaluator configuration, runtime revisions, judge configuration, and policy version. Verified policy versions retain their pinned benchmark sources and Harbor/Evalchemy commits.

EvalDash reads the StepSpec status file in each run's record directory. It withholds scores from running or failed steps while showing those states in run views. Shared measurement extraction reads record contents without depending on dashboard enrichment. Historical records without a step status retain their existing display.

A crash after writing a record but before StepRunner marks the step successful can rerun that evaluation. The [October 6, 2026 incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/627) showed a successful record replaced after a duplicate eval was cancelled.

The safe affected repository suite (`uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py`) passed 2,390 tests, with 3 skipped and 5 expected failures. Another 95 EvalDash tests passed. The four Docker-backed EvalDash kernel tests were not run here; their local PostgreSQL fixture timed out in an earlier attempt.

topics.title: [levanter] Replace the Pallas short convolution with a Triton kernel
topics.body:
Short convolutions on GPU run in a new streaming Triton kernel that reads each tensor once, instead of once per tap. The Pallas kernel is deleted, and the package moves from `levanter.kernels.pallas.short_conv` to `levanter.kernels.triton.short_conv`. In a single-GPU hero block, short-convolution time per step falls from 4.45 to 1.76 ms.

| Shape | Direction | Previous Pallas | Triton |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | forward | 423.9 us | 226.4 us |
| [16, 4096, 6144] | backward | 1024.3 us | 380.7 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | forward | 103.2 us | 59.3 us |
| [16, 4096, 1536] | backward | 262.9 us | 105.3 us |

Median kernel time per call on one GB200, 9 documents per sequence. The forward runs at the HBM floor of a read-one-write-one stream on the same tensor, and the backward at 1.14 times its floor. A port of the same algorithm to Pallas reached 230.0 and 403.7 us at C=6144, and needed code-generation workarounds (an inline-asm FMA, program ids clamped to the grid) that steer XLA's Triton pipeline.

The kernel takes kernel size 4, a channel count that is a multiple of 64, and bfloat16 or float32. The wrapper right-pads each local sequence to a multiple of 128 rows with the out-of-range segment id and drops the padded outputs, so any sequence length runs on the kernel. Other calls fall back to `short_conv_reference` with a warning. Every caller gets the kernel, so `GrugModelConfig.sconv_implementation` is removed; checkpoints are unchanged.

The forward and dx are bit-identical to `short_conv_reference` in bfloat16 and float32; dw changes only in fp32 summation order. On SM90 and newer the bf16 multiplies and adds are packed PTX (`mul.rn.bf16x2`, `add.rn.bf16x2`). Older GPUs take an fp32 op and a bf16 cast, which rounds the same way, and Triton's fp fusion is off so that LLVM cannot contract that fallback into a bf16 FMA that rounds once. The fallback has run on GB200 with the capability check forced, but not on an SM80 GPU.

Each program walks a sequence chunk of one channel block. It carries the previous three rows of x (in the backward also the next three rows of dy) and their segment ids in registers, and loads every row of a step before storing any; the backward writes one fp32 dw partial per chunk. A step whose rows lie in one document skips the segment masks, which cuts a backward step from 467 to 275 SASS instructions.

No rack run measured this kernel alone. On one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps), an earlier version that was 7-15% slower per call shortened the step by 0.55%.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

#!/bin/bash

# Research

MI350X reaches 3.86% MFU with bf16 Triton `ragged_dot`; its fp16 XLA runs reach 2.59–2.83%. The reported ~10 ms Triton expert matmul is a bottleneck hypothesis; the current MI350X results do not include a pinned-revision profile that attributes the full step. MI300X batch 32 reached 10.3% MFU over steps 2–9 but hung at step 10, which coincides with the trainer's watch interval; the cause and sustained throughput remain unconfirmed.

**Relevant code**
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L92-L108) — benchmark flags; no watch control
- [`synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/f8627e501110959b00c92ce30452bfaf780c95d9/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py#L145-L166) — trainer uses default watch configuration
- [`train.py#L641-L649`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/train.py#L641-L649) — interval selects watch computation
- [`ragged_dot.py#L341-L367`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/haliax/src/haliax/nn/ragged_dot.py#L341-L367) — XLA/Triton selection

# Proposed Fix

1. Extend the existing benchmark PR #9693 with a benchmark-only watch interval flag (0 disables watch) and the Slurm wrapper used in the issue. Pin one post-rebase benchmark commit and the ROCm/JAX versions for every comparison. Keep the production watch default unchanged.
2. On 8× MI300X, rerun the full EP8 batch-32 configuration for 20 steps with watch intervals 10 and 0, `RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=xla`, memory fraction 0.90, no profiler, and command buffers off. Record the step-10 outcome, median time over non-watch steps 2–9 and 11–19, tokens/s, MFU, and peak memory. Treat 10.3% as preliminary until a 20-step run completes; if both variants hang, capture the failing step's trace before changing the model.
3. At the same pinned commit, rerun MI350X bf16/Triton batch 8 and fp16/XLA batches 8, 16, and 32 with the same 20-step setup. Profile a separate run of the fastest completed configuration and report time in expert GEMMs, collectives, other kernels, and host gaps. Compare against the MI300X reference only after these reruns.
4. Use that profile to choose one next change: test `fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all` if communication dominates, or tune the Triton expert GEMM if it dominates. Test command-buffer types separately on a smaller shape with finite-loss checks before a full-model run; the [current ROCm setup](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/559) has produced non-finite gradients and crashes with command buffers enabled. Post each run's commit, exact command, job ID, step time, MFU, peak memory, and negative results here.

Completion criterion: a full 20-step MI350X run with finite loss and a measured improvement over the rerun bf16/Triton batch-8 baseline (previously 3.86%). #9777 already covers ROCm architecture parsing; RCCL ragged all-to-all remains unsupported in its reported test, so it is not a parallel implementation target for this issue.

🤖 ### MI350X bf16 matmul ceiling: 1,192 TFLOP/s in JAX (52% of datasheet peak), 1,261 sustained in PyTorch with TunableOp

Commits: 265ea0f (MAMF jobs 453328, 453329), d733a95 (453334), 52cf1ee (JAX 453412), 08516a7 (JAX 453420, 453421) · GPU: one MI350X or MI300X, whole node reserved · Scripts: [`experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/08516a7dd961b26fa87f5d9fe955493564175c7c/experiments/amd_matmul_ceiling) (PR #9840)

This measures how fast one GPU runs a plain dense matmul, to give the MFU numbers above a measured ceiling. Two tools ran on the same node for each GPU type: k007-002 for MI350X, k002-003 for MI300X. Both venvs install AMD's `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, which provides hipBLASLt; the nodes' system ROCm (`/opt/rocm-7.2.0`) is not used for compute.

- Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py) (PyTorch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0, `PYTORCH_TUNABLEOP_ENABLED=1`, which benchmarks every hipBLASLt kernel per shape) searches about 2,100 shapes. It reports MAMF (maximum achievable matmul FLOPS): the median of the 5 fastest of 200 iterations, run in bursts of 20 after 250 ms idle. It also reports MSMF (maximum sustainable matmul FLOPS): the best rate held for 2 s under continuous load.
- `jax_matmul.py` (JAX 0.11.0) times `jax.jit(jnp.matmul)` with XLA autotuning on: 1 s of warmup, then the median of ten 0.2 s windows of back-to-back calls. This is a sustained rate, so MSMF is the PyTorch number to compare it with.

- The best 10 JAX grid shapes in bf16 fall between 1,157 and 1,192 TFLOP/s.

Any hipBLASLt kernel is far faster than that, so level 0 appears to switch to a different GEMM path on ROCm, and it cannot measure hipBLASLt's untuned default choice.
- MAMF-finder's telemetry on MI350X read the wrong GPU. It samples `amdsmi` GPU 0, but HIP device 0 on k007-002 is PCI 0000:77:00, which is `amd-smi` GPU 3; `amd-smi` GPU 0 is an idle GPU at about 308 W. The 38 MHz and 308 W in the MI350X MAMF-finder logs, and its "not a boost burst" warning, come from that idle GPU. MAMF-finder's TFLOP/s do not depend on telemetry. On MI300X it reads 750 W and 1,315 MHz sustained and 2,096 MHz at boost, matching the 750 W cap in note 9 of Stas Bekman's table.
- Power cap on MI350X (`amd-smi static --limit`, job 453520): the socket power limit is 1,000 W, equal to the maximum limit and to the brochure's maximum TBP. During a sustained bf16 4096x4096x16384 matmul in JAX (job 453523), the GPU held 1,000 W at a 70-73 °C hotspot, below the 100 °C slowdown temperature, and its 8 compute dies ran at 1,332-1,513 MHz, about 1,400 MHz on average. At 1,400 MHz the peak formula (256 CUs x 4,096 bf16 FLOPs per clock) gives about 1,470 TFLOP/s, 64% of the 2.2 GHz figure. Against that power-limited peak, MSMF is about 86% and JAX in that run (1,145 TFLOP/s) 78%. MAMF's short bursts may run above the sustained clock before the GPU reaches its power limit, so the 1,400 MHz figure does not bound MAMF.
- With torch imported, the `amdsmi` Python binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` reports no GPUs, because torch has already loaded the ROCm SDK's own `libamd_smi.so.27`. `setup_envs.sh` uses the SDK's binding instead.

</details>

### MI350X Triton `ragged_dot` rewrite and tuning: batch 64 step 2.634 → 2.426 s, 8.58% → 9.32% MFU

Commit: 8471641 (local, not pushed) · GPU: MI350X ×8 · Jobs: 453565 (A/B), 453564 (microbenchmark), baseline 453384

PR: #9859 (AMD Instinct only; NVIDIA, TPU and megablox unchanged).

```bash
RAGGED_DOT_IMPL=triton XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.90 sbatch --export=ALL -N1 -p mi3508x -t 45 -o "logs/%x-%j.out" \
  experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/run_gpu.sh experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py --size full --steps 20 \
  --expert-axis 8 --watch-interval 0 --compilation-cache-dir $WORK/jax-cache --batch-size 64
```

| Step | Tokens/s | MFU | Peak mem |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.426 s (was 2.634) | 108,100 (was 99,500) | 9.32% (was 8.58%) | 184.2 GiB (unchanged) |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Loss matches the baseline to 4 decimals (11.7770 vs 11.7769 at step 19).
- Forward and dlhs now launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a device-side tile map, instead of a full row grid per expert. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. drhs uses an explicit flat grid. Rows past the last group are zero-filled.
- Tuned for MI350X: 256×256×64 tiles, 8 warps, 2 stages for forward and dlhs; 256×128×64, 4 warps, 1 stage for drhs; plus chiplet-aware program order. Blackwell, TPU and megablox are unchanged.
- Per call on one GPU at batch 64 (M=131072), before → after TFLOP/s:

  | Layout | w13 | w2 |
  |---|---|---|
  | fwd | 583 → 722 | 555 → 667 |
  | dlhs | 554 → 760 | 538 → 757 |
  | drhs | 410 → 581 | 396 → 573 |

- At batch 64 the tile map alone changes nothing. With the old blocks, w13 forward takes 2.95 ms either way. The gain there is block tuning. At batch 8 the tile map is a 4.6× win.
- `plgpu.CompilerParams` exposes only `num_warps` and `num_stages`, so AMD knobs (`waves_per_eu`, `matrix_instr_nonkdim`, `kpack`) can't be set from Pallas.
- drhs, at 573–581 TFLOP/s, is the remaining gap. Both of its operands are contraction-strided.

</details>

RCCL uses 112 channels, ring and the Simple protocol. The model's async EP all-gathers take 4.1 ms (about 280 GB/s) because they share compute units and HBM with concurrent compute: next to a matmul, an all-gather hides only 42% of it, even with the latency-hiding scheduler on.

The other 120 ms is async EP traffic not hidden by compute. The `msccl` f32 all-reduce kernels take under 2 ms.
- Pooled-wave moves about half the bytes of ring, but XLA leaves 130 of its 156 all-to-alls per step synchronous on the main stream with none of their time overlapped, and they launch 64 workgroups against 112. Exposed time is 402 ms. It also drops more assignments: 5.4% against ring's 0.9% at capacity factor 1.0.
- Against the old kernel (2.634 s), `save_moe` on the new kernel is 11.3% faster.

| GPU | Weight | Layout | Old (main) | New, generic config | New, tuned | Dense matmul |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| H100 | w13 | fwd | 3.556 / 483 | 3.473 / 495 | 2.855 / 602 | 2.421 / 710 |
| H100 | w13 | dlhs | 3.783 / 454 | 3.565 / 482 | 2.839 / 605 | 2.445 / 703 |
| H100 | w13 | drhs | 3.312 / 519 | 3.297 / 521 | 2.793 / 615 | 2.437 / 705 |
| GB200 | w13 | fwd | 2.377 / 723 | 1.719 / 1000 | 1.421 / 1209 | 1.243 / 1382 |
| GB200 | w13 | dlhs | 2.518 / 682 | 1.832 / 938 | 1.425 / 1206 | 1.218 / 1411 |
| GB200 | w13 | drhs | 1.829 / 939 | 1.826 / 941 | 1.469 / 1170 | 1.243 / 1382 |

<details><summary>Notes</summary>

- Numerics match the old kernel exactly in bf16. fwd and dlhs are bit-identical to XLA bf16. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are now zeros instead of NaN.
- `test_ragged_dot_dispatch.py`: 24 pass and 12 fail on both GPUs, all f32 layout cases. The cause is TF32 in Triton's `tl.dot`: the error is about 2.8e-4 against a 1e-4 tolerance, and the old kernel and XLA show the same. NVIDIA needs a looser f32 tolerance, or `input_precision="ieee"`.
- With the generic config, the new kernel is 1.0-2.1x faster at the June shapes (fwd and dlhs gain, drhs is flat), and 1.5-2.2x faster under skewed routing. At a Mixtral-like shape (G=8, 4096x14336) it is 0.68-1.67x, because `group_m=1` rereads the 117 MB expert weight for every row tile. `group_m` of 8-16 fixes that.

- Next steps: per-family NVIDIA configs, the f32 test fix, a model-level A/B on H100 and GB200, and a real B200 check.

</details>

topics.title: [grug] AdamH produces NaNs for zero-norm parameters
topics.body:
The AdamH copies used by current and historical Grug divide by `norm(new_p)` without a floor. A zero-norm matrix produces a NaN update even at learning rate zero. This poisoned a 67B SFT checkpoint on its first warmup update; the next forward pass reported NaN loss.

Reproduce:
1. Create a zero `2 x 2` parameter and an all-ones gradient.
2. Build `experiments.grug.moe.adamh.scale_by_adamh(learning_rate=0.0)` and apply one update.
3. Observe that every returned update is NaN. The vendored `experiments.june_tpu_67b_a2b.moe.adamh` copy behaves identically, including for stacked matrices.

Expected: zero-norm parameters remain finite under AdamH, including during a zero-learning-rate warmup step.

topics.title: [grug] Add the H100 pipeline foundation
topics.body:
Add a stage-local JAXPP pipeline for the full MoE model blocks, including latent/shared experts, SConv, attention positions and QB routing. Standard 1F1B remains the default. The synthetic runner supports the main recipe with FP32 parameters, BF16 compute and compute-scaled MuonH; the historical BF16 capacity recipe remains available.

Each routed expert parameter bank now shares one Frobenius norm across its experts, matching the stacked EP model. `--expert-normalization per_expert` provides an explicit comparison mode. `--qb-bias-mode frozen` retains the current pending QB bias while expert and router weights continue updating; adaptive QB remains the default. Numerical CPU regressions cover stacked-versus-stage-local updates and both QB state transitions.

The historical 48-layer, 65K synthetic diagnostic ran on 192 H100s with BF16-stored parameters and per-expert normalization. Its PP24/EP8/CP1 layout placed two layers in each stage and kept expert traffic within eight-GPU workers. It was chosen to establish capacity; no matched PP8/EP32/CP4 Megatron comparison was performed. The README records the later CP2 result and the differences in batch size and attention helpers. Historical hardware results do not validate the new normalization or frozen-QB option, and no SFT/RL quality comparison has been run.

The affected safe suite passed 2,391 tests with four skips and five expected failures. Focused CPU checks passed 86 tests with one skip; required lint, full type checking, strict docs and source links passed.

#9662 is stacked above this foundation and adds checkpoint/data support, the GB200 launcher, tracked runtime setup and bounded main-recipe hardware validation. Before merge, this foundation still owns replacing the positional result from `initialize_stage_local_pipeline_state`, centralizing the repeated backend/rematerialization identifiers, and separating the synthetic runner lifecycle in `pipeline_smoke.main`. These deferred changes require compiled-startup transport and optimizer-parking/warmup cleanup validation; #9662 then owns adapting its added checkpoint/data lifecycle.

topics.title: [grug] Add a Pallas-Triton flash attention for AMD GPUs
topics.body:
Add `gpu_pallas_triton_flash`, a fused causal attention for Grug on AMD GPUs, where Grug had no fused kernel. It is opt-in through `attention_implementation="gpu_pallas_triton_flash"` and changes no existing backend.

The kernel reduces each mask to one inclusive key lower bound per query, `max(segment start, q - W + 1)` for window `W`. Key blocks outside `[lower bound, q]` are skipped, and blocks fully inside it skip the mask computation. GQA indexes the shared KV head instead of repeating K/V. Forward, dQ and dK/dV are separate Pallas-Triton kernels, run per shard inside `shard_map` under a mesh. The FA4/CuTe wrapper and this one now share `levanter.sharding.partitioned_dims`.

On one MI350X at the June per-GPU shape (8 x 4096 tokens, 20 query heads, 5 KV heads, head_dim 128, bf16; job 453640), one layer's forward plus backward drops from 18.95 ms to 6.89 ms with a 2048-token window and from 18.98 ms to 10.92 ms causal. The full June model at batch 64 on 8x MI350X goes from 2.426 s to 1.853 s per step and from 9.32% to 12.20% MFU. Peak memory falls from 184 to 158 GiB, and the loss matches the reference run (job 453655 vs 453565). Details are in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027803714.

The value and gradient parity tests against `reference_attention` pass on MI350X and in the CPU Pallas interpreter there (jobs 453773 and 454023). CI runs the CPU tests.

Risks: JAX has deprecated the Pallas Triton backend. Each run of equal segment IDs is one document, so a segment ID that reappears after a different ID starts a new document; `reference_attention` lets the two runs attend to each other.

topics.title: [grug] Leave ragged MoE transport rows unwritten when nothing reads them
topics.body:
The ragged all-to-all MoE stops zero-filling and overwriting transport rows that no consumer reads, and on GPU builds its dispatch buffer with one scatter. Outputs, drops and gradients are bitwise unchanged. One MoE layer's forward and backward is 4.4-4.8% faster and its compiler temp 1.37 GB smaller, and the hero step shortens by 1.44% (13.737 to 13.542 s). The dispatch scatter, measured together with its backward use in #9833, shortened the step by a further 1.14%.

The expert chunks write disjoint rows of the dispatch and return buffers, but the custom VJP around `ragged_all_to_all` differentiated each write as an overwrite, so every layer's backward spent a [TK, H] select, add and zero fill on rows the next chunk would ignore. Each written row holds nothing before its one write, and for such a row an overwrite has the derivative of an add, so the transpose passes the output cotangent through unchanged. With every consumer reading only rows a collective wrote, the buffers need no fill: on GPU they come from a Triton kernel that writes nothing, elsewhere they are zero-filled. Each buffer is tied to a loop-carried value, because XLA would otherwise hoist an input-free buffer out of the layer loop and copy it into every layer's output slot. Dropped and padded slots get combine weight 0, and the combine and dispatch-gradient sums skip them. A GPU test fills every buffer with NaN instead of zero and requires identical outputs, drop counts and gradients.

On GPU, a Triton kernel builds the expert-sorted dispatch buffer by reading each token's row once and writing it to the token's accepted slots, where a gather read every row topk times: 0.535 ms (6.6 TB/s) at the hero's per-GPU routed shape (TK = 524288 rows of the 3072-wide latent). Its weighted form serves #9833's backward. The gather-sum's forward loops over 1024-wide hidden tiles, which keeps more programs resident: 0.508 ms against 0.574 ms.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [iris] Quarantine nodes with persistent isolated S3 failures
topics.body:
Add opt-in regional S3 read/write/delete probes to the Kubernetes node-agent so a node that remains Ready while storage requests stall can be quarantined before it receives more work. The probe uses the task storage environment, a tiny object per node incarnation, and a process deadline that bounds SDK retries and DNS stalls.

The controller cordons persistent failures only when a fresh majority of nodes successfully probed the same target after the failure began. A persistent cordon budget defaults to one node, and credential/configuration errors reset the failure streak. Node UID, boot ID, report freshness, and Kubernetes resource versions fence stale observations and concurrent operator changes.

Health and cordon evidence remain in node annotations even when Finelog is unavailable. Recovery requires an operator to uncordon the repaired node and release its budget annotation; running tasks are not evicted. Configuration, scratch-object lifecycle requirements, and recovery are documented in the CoreWeave guide.

Context: [node-local storage failure during the hero run](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/599).

topics.title: Score the first 4k Paloma PTB tokens in hero vibe checks
topics.body:
Add `paloma-ptb-first-4k` to the hero vibe-check prompt bank, following https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8827#issuecomment-5723229156. It tracks how the hero scores Paloma's Penn Treebank (PTB) text across sampled checkpoints.

The prompt is the first line of Paloma's `ptb` validation document, a single 399,782-character document with 87,132 tokens under the Marin tokenizer. The prompt is 17 tokens including BOS. The `expected` reference is the next 143 lines, or 4,056 tokens. With EOS, the prompt and reference total 4,074 tokens, within the sampler's 4,096-token `context_length`. Existing expected-answer scoring reports per-token probabilities and the total log-likelihood of the first ~4k PTB tokens at every sampled checkpoint. No code changes are needed. PTB is lowercase, with numbers replaced by `N` and rare words by `<unk>`, so the score partly measures in-context adaptation to that format.

Changing the prompt bank changes the sampling specification and creates a new request for every retained checkpoint. The hourly workflow in `next` mode keeps two jobs active, newest first. Steps 210000 and 204000, the two newest permanent checkpoints of `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k`, are sampled first. Older checkpoints backfill afterward at the saved priority.

All 47 prompts passed the sampler's prompt-prefix and context checks locally with the pinned tokenizer revision. `tests/hero_vibe_check/test_completions.py` had 19 passing tests. `./infra/pre-commit.py` passed on the changed file.

topics.title: [grafana] Prepare GPU history by requested priority
topics.body:
Prepare seven-day H100 and Blackwell (GB200) allocation-history panels grouped by each child job's requested priority. An Interactive request dispatched as Batch stays in the Interactive group. There is no applied-priority lookup or toggle. Iris and Finelog server code, persisted schemas, retention and writes are unchanged.

The projection sums requested GPU sizes over recorded attempt execution intervals at common sampling instants, with cadence chosen from the selected range: one minute through six hours, five minutes through two days, and fifteen minutes through seven days. Exact historical pod binding/cleanup intervals and allocatable capacity remain unavailable. The requested-GPU series therefore recovers only part of allocation; every point is marked incomplete and idle stays blank. Missing regional inputs leave blank spans. Coverage compares Finelog per-root Running task counts with retained attempt intervals, including CPU tasks; differences flag incomplete or inconsistent task history. It also reports setup tasks and unresolved GPU models. Without assignment creation times, the reader cannot establish when setup began, so setup GPU quantities stay blank.

The production metadata reader remains to be implemented and wired; without one the bridge returns HTTP 503. An approved temporary pilot used Grafana's actual CW service identity plus five-minute Iris dashboard-role cookies over the public Kubernetes controller proxy in all three regions. Existing job/resource/full-retry reads succeeded, GetCurrentUser reported dashboard, and SELECT1 was denied by Iris with HTTP 403. All temporary Role/RoleBinding objects were deleted and absence verified; Grafana's original proxy403 returned afterward. No production grants, credentials or deployment remain from the pilot. The minimal tested transport scope is services/proxy on iris/iris-controller-svc:10000; this reader's POST RPCs need the Kubernetes create verb, plus separate read-only Iris authentication.

A straightforward job/task-API reader would require at least 44,398 inventory calls over the captured sampled cohort, before additional pages and full-retry calls. This is a request-count estimate, not measured production latency. Existing controller backups offer a possible bulk alternative without controller changes: recent backups exist in all three regions. One GB200 backup was 25.4 MB compressed and 421.6 MB decompressed; it downloaded in 1.17s, decompressed in 0.22s, and returned 5,712 retained attempts in a 0.032s immutable local SQL query on devbox. Regional coverage, Cloud Run memory/refresh cost, and scoped object-read credentials still need validation before choosing and wiring that reader. Existing backups already contain requested band and current task band; older attempts do not have their own applied-band field.

All 421 Grafana tests and pre-commit checks passed. The requested-only preview uses captured task-state and regional metadata, with 672 common fifteen-minute instants per model. Every point is incomplete; 226 instants show a difference between per-root Running counts and retained intervals. Earlier applied-view replay timings are retained as prior measurements; production requested-reader loading and refresh costs remain unmeasured.

topics.title: Pod creation fails on a node with 65K empty Silo cgroups
topics.body:
On October 2, new pods failed to start on CoreWeave node `g5bc6da`, blocking new jobs. Kubernetes reported `no space left on device` while creating a pod’s cgroup, the kernel group used to track and limit container resources. The node still reported healthy, and its filesystem had 3.55 TB free.

The host cgroup tree had 65,535 descendant groups. Of these, 65,412 were under `/silo`; that entire subtree contained no processes. This strongly suggests exhaustion of the kernel’s roughly 64K memory-cgroup ID space, though we have not traced the failing allocator.

Silo is the nested container runtime running inside our privileged Iris job `muchanem.cap-pipeline-host-53`. Two sampled container IDs from its `containerd-shim` processes matched empty `/silo` cgroups. This points to a cleanup problem in that workload’s runtime, but we have not identified the code path responsible. We have no evidence that CoreWeave’s host containerd created these groups.

Please investigate whether completed containers leave cgroups and shim processes behind, and fix the cleanup path. Verify that repeated container creation and teardown do not keep increasing either count. Coordinate cleanup of the affected node with the pipeline owner; an empty cgroup alone does not establish that it is safe to remove while the runtime is active.

---

topics.title: 🤖 Inference workers can collide on ports and fail evals
topics.body:
Two inference jobs on the same node can select the same localhost port. The port-selection helper closes its socket before vLLM starts, leaving the port unreserved. Readiness accepts any successful `/v1/models` response without checking the model.

This broke North Mini Code’s MRCR-32k eval: both inference jobs selected `127.0.0.1:39535` on `g1cbf32`. North accepted Nemotron’s server as ready, then all 602 requests failed with “model does not exist” errors.

Reproduce:

1. Start two inference jobs concurrently on the same node.
2. If their ports collide, one job’s readiness check can accept the other job’s server while its own model is still loading.

Expected: each inference job serves its configured model, and readiness verifies that model.

[Logs, source links, and socket reproduction](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/662).

comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The inference launch path probes an ephemeral port, closes the socket, then starts vLLM; concurrent jobs can select the same port before either server listens. Readiness accepts any HTTP 200 from `/v1/models`, so a job can advertise its requested alias while forwarding to another model. [The incident record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/662) captured this on `g1cbf32`.

**Relevant code**
- [`vllm_backend.py#L57`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_backend.py#L57) — released port probe
- [`iris.py#L435`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L435) — direct job submission
- [`iris.py#L507`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/iris.py#L507) — broker worker submission
- [`port_allocator.py#L19`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/worker/port_allocator.py#L19) — task port allocation
- [`vllm_server.py#L642`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/inference/vllm_server.py#L642) — HTTP readiness probe

# Proposed Fix

`run_iris_service()` and `_run_broker_worker()` reach `_prepared_local_inference()`, which currently leaves vLLM to probe its own port. Request a named backend port at each Iris job submission and pass that task-owned port into local inference; then require the configured served model ID in `/v1/models` before declaring vLLM ready. Add a local fake-server regression for a wrong-model readiness response.

🤖 PR #9863 allocates task-owned backend ports for direct and brokered Iris inference jobs and requires the configured model in vLLM readiness responses. The safe inference and Fray suites passed (179 tests), and lint and type checks passed. CI and review are in progress.

topics.title: [grug] Hide the hero's bare MoE transports behind shared and chunk GEMMs
topics.body:
Under the hero's carry offload, every MoE transport except one ~1 ms routing-weight return now runs beside a GEMM, which shortens the step by 0.73% (12.730 to 12.638 s) and cuts exposed collective time from 1.19 to 0.85 s/step. Before, with one collective in flight, the first forward dispatch and both recomputed dispatches of the backward ran bare (0.63 s/step), and small collectives inside the routed-MoE section held the slot through expert GEMMs. Three changes that only work together fix the schedule:

- The MLP section's FSDP weight all-gathers, the QB router statistics and the drop count complete before the first dispatch. The statistics are saved for the backward, so its recompute does not rerun their all-reduces.
- The routed MoE runs caller work beside its first dispatch (`DispatchOverlap`), and the block hands it the first shared expert's gate/up projections. Barriers order the remaining transports so that each has an expert or chunk GEMM beside it, in the forward and in the backward's recompute.
- Each layer's carry offload copy starts after the layer's weight slices. XLA puts the 4.3 ms carry copy and the slices on the same memcpy streams in program order, and without this ordering the weight prefetch lands a slice behind the copy and stalls the layer (98-152 ms/step on the production wheel). On #9708's head, disabling only this ordering slowed the step by 0.79%.

Configurations without the carry offload keep the plain path. Neither path is safe under XLA's default scheduler, which can start two transports together, so the launcher refuses a ragged carry-offload run whose XLA flags switch the latency-hiding scheduler off. `forward_barrier` is an `optimization_barrier` whose backward passes cotangents straight through, so a weight gradient's all-reduce and FSDP slice still fuse into a reduce-scatter.

In a four-GPU gate, loss and drop counts are bitwise unchanged and gradients change at rounding level, within the difference between two runs of the same code. In the hero the carry ordering also moves fusion boundaries, so its forward changes at rounding level.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Fuse the expert dSwiGLU and skip recomputed pre-activation stores
topics.body:
Two changes to the routed experts' QuACK kernels, each bitwise or within bf16 rounding:

| Change | Kernel | Hero step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SwiGLU backward and the routing-weight row dot in the dh GEMM's epilogue | 3.54 ms against 5.10 ms per expert chunk | 13.059 to 12.943 s (+0.89%) |
| No gate/up pre-activation store in a forward whose residuals are recomputed | 6.14 ms against 6.48 ms per median chunk, 96 chunks per step | 12.652 to 12.611 s (+0.33%) |

The expert MLP backward wrote dh = dy @ W2^T to HBM and read it back with the gate/up pre-activations in an elementwise pass for the SwiGLU backward and the row dot <h, dh>. A QuACK epilogue on the grouped dh GEMM now unpacks the interleaved (gate, up) tile, applies the SwiGLU backward to the fp32 accumulator, writes the packed (d_gate, d_up) and reduces the row dot, so dh is never materialized. Outputs, drops and dW2 are bitwise unchanged; dx, dW13 and dS change at bf16 rounding (median ~1 ulp), because the SwiGLU backward runs on the unrounded accumulator.

Under the hero's layer remat, the forward's gated GEMM wrote the [C, 2I] pre-activations of every chunk, which the backward recomputes. `_routed_experts` declares `optimize_remat`, so such a forward runs a primal that calls the expert MLP's new `apply`, which returns the output alone, and the gated GEMM gains a launcher that never writes the pre-activations. Each chunk's dispatch still waits on the previous chunk's gate/up output. The forward is bitwise unchanged, and removing the change from all of #9708 slowed the step by 0.47%.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

topics.title: [grug] Add GB200 launch and H100 validation support
topics.body:
Stack the GB200 launcher, checkpoint/data support and H100 validation runner on the pipeline foundation in #9279 for the model recipe from main `89ac0d770506f7e27ca217760ec5ca3246694e7e`. The launcher uses FP32 parameters, BF16 compute, compute-scaled MuonH, SM100 ragged transport and Flash Attention. It requests one hard NVLink domain in the opportunistic BATCH queue and separates queue wait from worker execution deadlines. Future run names use `pipeline-gb200-*` or `pipeline-h100-*`.

Executable `0da04acccf7b0842319a8668d71ccc697a7b10ec` completed the corrected eight-GB200 synthetic gate with two full-width layers, PP2/EP4 and sequence length 4096. The two losses were 11.806337356567383 and 0.4912489652633667. All eight native GPU processes, both Iris GPU tasks and the coordinator exited zero. All 48 startup task ABI records had zero input memory-kind mismatches. Both coordinator failure and preemption retry caps were zero; the SDK launch example sets both explicitly because the CLI retry option controls failure retries only. [GB200 setup and standalone commands](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/experiments/grug/moe_hero_pipeline/GB200.md) record prerequisites and acceptance criteria.

The combined H100 runner was validated at `a1e3ab278eeb05bb645db641dd3e7dabedf90dbb` on 16 H100s with two full-width layers, PP2/EP8 and sequence length 4096. Ten synthetic updates had finite losses from 11.804966926574707 to 0.4793720245361328. Twenty fresh Harrier updates consumed 2,621,440 tokens with finite losses from 11.8075590133667 to 7.612007141113281. All 200 raw components remained nonempty with their original mixture weights and order. Both GPU tasks and supervisors exited zero; fresh-data logs retain 15 individual rank exits, while the supervisor's child-reaping contract certifies all 16. No checkpoint was written in those full-width trials. Save/restore support is included, but hardware checkpoint validation is limited to the historical reduced-model comparison: a 90,018,826-byte scratch checkpoint and a resumed-versus-uninterrupted loss difference of 9.5367431640625e-7, within unchanged 1e-5 tolerances. The current full-width main-recipe checkpoint path has not been validated on GPUs. These runs used the explicit SM90 pooled-wave/FA4 adapter with SYRK disabled and establish no H100 ragged-transport parity. [H100 reference](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/codex/hero-gb200-pipeline/docs/references/hero-pipeline-h100.md) separates these runs from the historical reduced-model checkpoint comparison.

The runtime pins upstream JAXPP `328f75a80cecf22c7cc030a82d8941d3c1e220b6` plus a tracked host-memory/startup overlay. JAX 0.11.1 overrides JAXPP's declared compatibility cap and remains experimental; CUDA dependencies with lower bounds are recorded per launch. Installer recovery avoids duplicate global reinstall flags, including on deployed older worker wrappers. The [Iris installer incident record](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/600) distinguishes the initiating GitHub fetch failure from the broken recovery command. Main-recipe argument parsing rejects AdamW before distributed initialization. Shared pipeline configuration, process ownership, array predicates, data scheduling and loader cleanup consolidate the overlapping work from #9279 and #9460.

#9279 contains the shared expert-bank normalization correction, FP32 main-recipe precision and optional frozen QB bias, together with their CPU regressions and historical layout explanation. The hardware gates used FP32 parameters and BF16 compute, with per-expert normalization and adaptive QB. They do not validate the shared-bank normalization correction or frozen-QB mode.

The combined executable, runtime and test source is identical to the previously published `5c2d91a6e48a43573b7f0b09be7e5f16bfc3eddc` snapshot. The README now selects per-expert normalization explicitly in its historical reproduction command. Required lint, type checks, hooks, strict docs and source-link checks passed on that source. The affected safe suite passed 5,566 tests with 18 skips and six expected failures, using library imports from the current checkout. topics.title: [haliax] Add tile-map Triton ragged_dot kernels for AMD Instinct GPUs
topics.body:
On AMD Instinct GPUs, `ragged_dot(..., implementation="triton")` now runs a second family of Pallas-Triton grouped-GEMM kernels, called tile-map kernels. NVIDIA GPUs, TPU and megablox behave exactly as before. NVIDIA keeps the existing group-grid kernels and block sizes, including the Blackwell `block_n` of 256. Those kernels are unchanged in the diff. `_TILE_MAP_GPU_FAMILIES` lists the GPU families that use the tile-map kernels. Adding NVIDIA to it is a one-line change, for a follow-up once H100 and B200 have been measured.

The existing kernels give every group a full grid over all row tiles and exit early on most of them. In the tile-map kernels, the forward and input-gradient (dlhs) kernels launch one program per (group, row tile, column tile) from a tile map built on device from `group_sizes`, as in megablox's `make_group_metadata`. dlhs reads the weights transposed in place, with no `rhs.mT` copy. The weight gradient (drhs) uses one flat grid over all groups. Rows past `sum(group_sizes)` are zero-filled. The old kernels leave them unwritten. Block sizes come from a per-GPU-family table that was swept on MI350X. Two launch-order options are new: chiplet-aware program numbering (`num_xcds`) and grouped tile rows (`group_m`).

Per-call times on one MI350X, bf16, balanced groups. Each cell is TFLOP/s for the old kernels, then the new ones (job 453824). The June expert shapes are G=32, with w13 at K=N=2560 and w2 at K=1280, N=2560.

| Shape | M | fwd | dlhs | drhs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| June w13 | 16384 | 94 → 594 | 88 → 635 | 378 → 483 |
| June w13 | 131072 | 587 → 730 | 556 → 808 | 428 → 585 |
| June w13 | 196608 | 525 → 735 | 511 → 818 | 429 → 579 |
| June w2 | 131072 | 560 → 668 | 541 → 765 | 403 → 586 |
| Mixtral-like w1, G=8, 4096x14336 | 16384 | 425 → 771 | 383 → 861 | 435 → 593 |
| Mixtral-like w1 | 65536 | 629 → 792 | 596 → 898 | 449 → 591 |

A dense `jnp.matmul` with the same FLOPs runs at about 730-960 TFLOP/s on this GPU. A sweep of `group_m` from 1 to 16 and `num_xcds` of 1 or 8 ran at both shape sets. Every setting beat the old kernels, and the chosen AMD entries are within 5% of the best setting sampled.

The full June model ran on 8x MI350X with EP8, `gpu_pallas_triton_flash` attention, memory fraction 0.90 and 20 steps. The table gives the median step over steps 2-19:

| Remat | Batch | Old kernels | New kernels | Peak memory (new) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| recompute_all | 64 | 2.149 s (122.0k tok/s) | 1.853 s (141.5k tok/s) | 158.4 GiB |
| recompute_all | 96 | 3.080 s (127.7k tok/s) | 2.696 s (145.9k tok/s) | 164.7 GiB |
| save_moe | 64 | 1.988 s (131.9k tok/s) | 1.832 s (143.1k tok/s) | 205.8 GiB |
| save_moe | 96 | 2.867 s (137.2k tok/s) | 2.672 s (147.2k tok/s) | 235.7 GiB |

Step-19 loss agrees with the old kernels within 1e-4. Earlier batch-96 runs on these kernels took 4.5-5.0 s per step, and one ran out of memory. Those runs reused XLA autotuning results from the per-fusion autotune cache, which JAX keeps inside `--compilation-cache-dir`. With that cache off (`JAX_PERSISTENT_CACHE_ENABLE_XLA_CACHES=none`) or empty, batch 96 runs at 2.66-2.70 s and its throughput is above batch 64. The kernels were not the cause: per call they are 25-35% faster at batch 96's M=196608. With a warm autotune cache, save_moe at batch 64 took 4.95 s per step on the new kernels and 5.62 s on the old ones. With fresh autotuning it took 1.83 s and 1.99 s. Jobs: 453914, 453961 and 453944 (A/B), 453791 and 453823 (cache reproduction).

`lib/levanter/scripts/bench/bench_ragged_dot_triton.py` times both kernel families, XLA and a dense matmul, and sweeps tile-map block configs. The edge-case tests (empty groups, unaligned boundaries, rows past the last group, partial tiles, every VJP layout) run for both families on a GPU. The tile-map family also runs them on CPU through the Pallas interpreter. Tests passed on MI350X (job 453882) and on the CPU interpreter (job 453881). f32 cases skip on NVIDIA, because Triton runs f32 dots in TF32 there.

Background and earlier measurements: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9812#issuecomment-6027367267

Part of #9812

topics.title: [experiments] Measure the dense matmul ceiling on AMD Instinct GPUs
topics.body:
Add scripts that measure the dense matmul throughput one AMD Instinct GPU reaches, so the MFU numbers in #9812 can be read against a measured ceiling instead of only the datasheet peak. They run on the AMD HPC Fund cluster under Slurm.

Two measurements run on the same node, which the README pins with `-w`. Stas Bekman's [MAMF-finder](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/benchmarks/mamf-finder.py), pinned to commit 0359db8, searches about 2,100 GEMM shapes in PyTorch with TunableOp. It reports the best short-burst rate (MAMF) and the best rate held for 2 s (MSMF). `jax_matmul.py` times `jnp.matmul` through XLA over a shape grid or a shapes file, which is the path our training uses. Both venvs install the `rocm-sdk-libraries==10.0.0` wheel, so PyTorch and JAX get hipBLASLt from the same package.

On MI300X, MAMF-finder gives 698 TFLOP/s MAMF and 645 MSMF in bf16. That is within 3.3% of the MI300X row in Stas Bekman's [published table](https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering/blob/0359db89793c313e90e4f8a8bc8a2b1514ba00ae/compute/accelerator/README.md#maximum-achievable-and-sustainable-matmul-flops-comparison-table) (676 and 659), so the setup reproduces his. On MI350X in bf16, MAMF is 1,445 TFLOP/s and MSMF 1,261. On the same node, JAX reaches 1,192, which is 52% of the 2,307 TFLOP/s datasheet peak. At MAMF's best shape, 4608x4096x7168, JAX runs at 80% of MSMF. JAX throughput on the same shapes differed by up to 8% between two MI350X nodes. Full results, versions and job IDs are in #9812.

`setup_envs.sh` uses the ROCm SDK's own `amdsmi` binding. With torch imported, the binding from `/opt/rocm-7.2.0` loads a second `libamd_smi` and reports no GPUs, which left MAMF-finder without power and clock telemetry. The batch scripts pass `--no-requeue` because the cluster requeues failed jobs onto other nodes by default.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [grug] Resume Hero pipeline checkpoints
topics.body:
Save and resume Hero pipeline model parameters, optimizer state, and pending QB router updates through Levanter's completed `step-N` checkpoints. The stage-independent tree uses global layer paths and restores into the compiled MPMD placement, including pinned-host optimizer state; unused compiled input leaves retain their initialized placement so saved values remain representable. `--steps` remains the total training schedule length across restarts.

CPU AdamW continuation after restoring step 2 matches uninterrupted steps 3 and 4 bit for bit, including parameters, optimizer state, and pending router updates, with both two-stage and five-stage destination layouts. The changing learning-rate schedule detects reset optimizer counters. AdamW and MuonH state round trips also pass across stage splits. After merging the latest #9279 base, the Hero pipeline and argument modules have 15 passing tests; the affected safe suite has 2,435 passes, four skips, and five expected failures. Lint and type checks pass.

On two H100x8 nodes, a reduced-width four-layer pipeline saved step 1, restored it, and completed step 2. Resumed step-2 loss was 6.94263744 versus 6.94263697 in an uninterrupted control (absolute difference 4.77e-7). A separate two-layer, full-width Hero probe (d6144, 384 experts) at sequence length 4096 also saved step 1 and resumed through step 2. Resumed step-2 loss was 11.56717205 versus 11.56716919 in its uninterrupted control (absolute difference 2.86e-6). All six save, resume, and control jobs completed with finite losses and both Iris and native worker exits at zero. Both configurations used PP2, EP8, BF16 MuonH, and pinned-host optimizer state. Checkpoints were written only to scratch storage. These historical GPU probes predate the latest base updates to expert normalization and the FP32 main recipe; they do not validate those updates.

These are bounded checks; the full 48-layer, 65K-token Hero training shape has not been checkpointed and resumed. The GPU probes used the pinned JAXPP build plus local offload and DIME patches required by the Hero pipeline; durable upstream support remains a dependency of #9279. Existing Hero FSDP checkpoints have a different stacked state tree with optional master and EMA weights and are not importable by this runner. Stacked on #9279.

topics.title: [grug] Raise hero single-rack MFU from 28.2% to 31.2%
topics.body:
On one GB200 NVL72 rack, these commits shorten the `moe_hero_ep` training step from 13.90 to 12.59 s (28.24% to 31.18% MFU), with loss inside the run-to-run noise of unchanged code. The PGLE profile builder adds no change by default; with a profile built from the program's own trace, the tip before the last two commits ran 12.515 s/step (31.37% MFU, +0.77% over 12.611 without a profile). The changes come from profiling the step's most expensive scopes and from benchmarking OLMo-core 3's BF16 MoE kernels against this path (#9636).

Each row is one run on one rack (`cw-us-east-08a`, 64 GPUs), restored from `hero-fa4sm100-nomask-step146k` step 180000 with seed 0 for 100 steps, on main's production PJRT wheel. The time is the median step over steps 180011-180099 without the three profiled steps; the gain is the previous row's time divided by this row's, minus one. Repeated runs of the same code differ by about 0.1%. The runs predate the final refactors and review fixes, and the hero's train step lowers to identical StableHLO before and after them.

| Change | Commit | s/step | MFU | Gain |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| main | b4d1761ff2 | 13.899 | 28.24% | |
| Remat discounts the host-offloaded carry | 13448300c6 | 13.737 | 28.57% | +1.18% |
| Unfilled ragged transport buffers | a544f2571c | 13.542 | 28.99% | +1.44% |
| Expert-side routing-weight gradient | 9383ef90cc | 13.130 | 29.90% | +3.14% |
| Streaming Triton short convolution | 5600e67b2e | 13.059 | 30.06% | +0.55% |
| SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM epilogue | c573fecfe0 | 12.943 | 30.33% | +0.89% |
| Device-side kernel availability check | 99d961ed43 | | | no hero change |
| Triton router top-k | 7d28781d70 | 12.875 | 30.49% | +0.53% |
| Token-major dispatch scatter | 3ebb6f91b1 | 12.730 | 30.83% | +1.14% |
| Shared and chunk GEMMs under the MoE transports | a225408148 | 12.638 | 31.06% | +0.73% |
| Synchronous collectives without the carry offload | 7caae09edc | | | no hero change |
| Shared-expert SwiGLU in QuACK epilogues | b24cfe37f8 | 12.652 | 31.03% | -0.11% |
| No routed pre-activation store under remat | 332b1f0b02 | 12.611 | 31.13% | +0.33% |
| PGLE profile builder | 379fdf0e66 | | | no hero change by default |
| End-to-end test that no transport consumer reads unwritten rows | ea02772298 | | | no hero change |
| Short conv and router top-k in Pallas instead of raw Triton | 729a0757f4, fea1451269 | 12.591 | 31.18% | +0.15% |
| Packed bf16 short-conv rounding only on SM90 and newer | 088095b07f | | | no hero change |
| Poisoning test retraces its recompute for each fill | 2b159517c1 | | | no hero change |

The scheduling row bundles three changes that do not stand alone. The MLP-section weight prefetch (from #9481) lets the first shared expert's gate/up projection run beside the first ragged dispatch, but it puts a weight slice behind each layer's carry-offload copy on the same memcpy stream, which stalls the forward by 98-152 ms/step. A barrier that issues the slices before the copy removes the stall; disabling it at the tip slows the step by 0.79%. The shared-expert QuACK row is negative because the scheduling row relies on the shared GEMMs to cover the transports: the 0.18 s/step of compute it saves exposes 0.24 s/step of transport. Removing it from the tip still slows the step, by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs.

The last row's gain is against a fresh run of the previous tip, 12.610 s/step, made beside it. Its kernels compile through the same Triton compiler: per call on GB200 the short convolution's forward and backward take 230 and 404 us against 244 and 449 us at 6,144 channels, and the top-k 0.107 against 0.127 ms. Pallas also lets the kernels' tests run on CPU through its interpreter.

Each change that gained less than about 0.3% was removed from the tip and kept only if the tip then slowed by more than 0.2%, with a second pair for results between 0.2% and 0.4%. This dropped a scatter-based inverse permutation (the tip was 0.04% faster without it) and a Triton bincount (0.22% and 0.10%), and kept the pre-activation change (0.47%). The rows from the unfilled transport buffers through the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward were measured with the inverse permutation in their base; without it, the last of them ran the same 12.943 s.

The unfilled transport buffers, top-k kernel, dispatch scatter and pre-activation change are bitwise, as is the Pallas top-k; the Pallas short convolution keeps its forward and `dx` bitwise, with its weight gradient within fp32 summation-order rounding. The routing-weight gradient, the dh-epilogue SwiGLU backward and the short convolution's weight gradient change at bf16 rounding. The shared-expert SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator, which changes 0.06-0.3% of downstream routing assignments and stays as close to an fp32 reference as before; the carry barrier moves fusion boundaries. Over 100 steps the tip's loss differs from main by at most 3.8e-4 (2.6e-4 with the profile), against 3.3e-4 between two runs of main.

`moe_mlp` and `MoEExpertMlp` gain `routing_weight_gradient`. The default, `EXACT`, keeps the expert outputs for the backward. `EXPERT_SIDE` takes the gradient from the expert MLP's own backward and skips storing and returning the outputs, but the gradient is zero or inexact wherever `w * dout` rounds to zero in the cotangent dtype, as at a zero weight or a small float16 product. The hero selects `EXPERT_SIDE` (positive sigmoid weights, bf16 cotangents); other ragged users keep `EXACT`.

Peak HBM rises from 103.1 to 123.2 GiB of a 143.75 GiB pool, mainly the 18 GiB routed MoE output the hero saves for the backward; under the carry offload the launcher defaults to `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION=0.78` and slop 105, validated on one rack. A ragged run without the carry offload keeps XLA's default scheduler, which ignores the one-collective limit, so it now runs collectives synchronously; the hero always offloads. A PGLE profile matches one program and mesh, so the production run needs its own before it gains the profile's 0.77%; automatic PGLE stays off. Giving host transfers their own memcpy streams in the PJRT wheel would remove the copy collision for any program; that is left for a follow-up.

This supersedes #9481. It carries that PR's mirror transpose parameters, weight prefetch and PGLE builder, and replaces its two-stage chunk pipelining with the dispatch overlap above, which with PGLE measured 12.666 s/step against 12.783 for pipelining with PGLE on a PJRT wheel without the copy stall, both before the kernels above. Part of #9636; the OLMo-core comparison is on that issue, and the research records are `.agents/logbooks/mfu30.md` and `.agents/logbooks/olmo9636.md` on `research/mcwitt/mfu30`.

topics.title: [grug] Add a gather MoE combine and a Triton routing top-k for ROCm
topics.body:
On ROCm, replace the ring EP MoE scatter-add combine with a gather, and replace `jax.lax.top_k` in `QBRoutedMoE` routing with a Pallas-Triton kernel. Both are selected only when `is_rocm_backend()` is true. TPU and NVIDIA keep the scatter-add combine and `jax.lax.top_k`.

On AMD GPUs the combine `zeros_like(x_global).at[token_local].add(...)` and the transpose of the dispatch `jnp.take` compile to scatter-adds that run at about 0.8-1.2 TB/s. `jax.lax.top_k` over the router matrix lowers to rocprim radix sorts.

The ring path builds an inverse map from each (token, k) assignment to the dispatch slot that holds it. The dispatch take and the combine get custom VJPs, so both directions are gathers: each token sums its at most K slot rows in f32 (K = 4 in the June model). The combine output is bit-identical to an f32 scatter-add rounded to bf16. The top-k kernel reads each router row once and runs K rounds of max plus lowest index of the max over total-order integer keys. Its indices match `lax.top_k`, ties included. Values are gathered outside the kernel, so gradients match `lax.top_k`.

Single-MI350X microbenchmark at June per-GPU shapes (`bench_grug_ring_combine_top_k.py`, job 453908):

| | scatter / `lax.top_k` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| combine forward | 2.420 ms | 0.969 ms |
| dispatch + combine, forward and backward | 5.436 ms | 1.790 ms |
| routing top-5 of 256, 32,768 tokens | 0.435 ms | 0.048 ms |

Full June model, batch 64, flash attention, 8x MI350X, fresh compiles, step time:

| remat policy | before | after | jobs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `save_moe` | 1.823 s (12.40% MFU) | 1.735 s (13.03% MFU) | 453972 / 453979 |
| `recompute_all` | 1.848 s | 1.788 s | 453841 / 453957 |

Losses agree within 4e-4. These runs used the flash attention from #9853 and the tuned Triton `ragged_dot` from #9859. This PR does not depend on either.

On 8x MI350X (job 454059), `test_routing_top_k.py` passes 13 of 13 and `test_grugformer_moe.py` passes 71 with 5 failures; under `JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu` both files pass. The 5 failures are the ragged all-to-all tests, such as `test_moe_ep_path_lowers_on_abstract_mesh[ragged_all_to_all]`: `ep_ragged_all_to_all.py` cannot parse `gfx950` as a compute capability. The same 5 tests fail on `main` (job 454060).

The dispatch selection `top_k` and the QB threshold `top_k` still use rocprim sorts, about 12 ms and 8 ms per step. The gather combine has not been measured on TPU or NVIDIA.

Part of #9812

topics.title: [grug] Run the shared experts' SwiGLU in QuACK GEMM epilogues
topics.body:
The hero's shared experts run their gate/up and down projections as QuACK GEMMs with SwiGLU and its backward in the epilogues: forward and backward of one shared expert take 13.93 ms instead of 14.51 ms at the hero's per-GPU shape (65536 tokens, width 6144, intermediate width 3072). Removing the change from all of #9708 slows the step by 0.35% and 0.22% in two pairs of runs.

With every PR of this stack and #9829, one 64-GPU hero rack ran 12.590 s/step (31.18% MFU), against 13.899 s (28.24% MFU) for main at #9708's base, with loss within 4.9e-4 of a run of #9708.

Each shared expert runs as two per-shard ops: a gate/up GEMM against interleaved weights with SwiGLU in its epilogue, returning the pre-activations and h, and a down op whose backward runs the SwiGLU backward in the dh GEMM's epilogue. dx and the gate/up weight gradient are single GEMMs on the interleaved layout. The split keeps the gate/up projection movable, so #9835 can run the first shared expert's gate/up beside the first dispatch. The weights stay separate FSDP leaves, gathered inside the shard map, so their gradients still reduce-scatter. Without QuACK, for another activation, or for operands other than bfloat16, the same ops run as XLA einsums.

Since only the down op reads h, the gate/up op stops h's gradient; otherwise the dispatch overlap would hand back dense zeros for h and the backward would run a SwiGLU backward over [T, 2I] per layer that adds nothing. SwiGLU now runs on the fp32 accumulator. Against an fp32 reference in a 4-GPU model gate, the loss error moves from 5.1e-5 to 4.5e-5 and the shared-expert gradient error from 1.22e-2 to 1.15e-2.

Directly on #9835 the change measured -0.11% (12.638 to 12.652 s): there the shared GEMMs cover the transports, and the shorter GEMMs left 0.24 s/step more transport exposed. Measured without #9835 it gained 0.72%, with peak HBM 123.4 to 121.9 GiB.

The QuACK availability check moves to `levanter.grug._moe.availability` and asks the default device for its platform. The shared experts' kernel selection calls it outside the ragged backend, where a test that stubs `jax.default_backend` on CPU devices would make the old check's `jax.devices("gpu")` raise.

Step times are single runs on one 64-GPU hero rack (restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps) from #9708's measurements.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [eval] Check in the September evaluation campaign
topics.body:
Check in the model, evaluator, and launcher configurations for the September 2026 evaluation campaign, together with the runtime fixes needed for serving, retry, resume, and coverage. The launcher validates external pins, writes immutable effective-config snapshots, and accepts an optional submitter-controlled version label. That label does not attest policy conformance.

Harbor results are bound to the full model and hosted judge configurations, dataset, policy, runtime, and task limit. Resume checks this identity before submission and reuse. A changed checkpoint under the same served name is rejected, as are existing roots without model-bound provenance. Recovery retries known infrastructure failures and unscored trials while retaining scored outcomes and unknown errors.

The frozen Harbor runtime pins 94b118022fe3e677784a638daf33d57a836fa5fe and includes the Tau3 adapter. The Evalchemy lock and generated pin match Marin's external dependency configuration.

SWE-bench uses the native Mini-SWE adapter from merged [Harbor #232](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/232) and [#233](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/233). Its 32,768-token context includes the prompt and reply together. Mini-SWE counts the rendered prompt through the serving tokenizer, including tools and the generation prefix, and caps the reply within the remaining budget and server window. Harbor loads Mini-SWE's base configuration before applying overrides and selects its batch agent, which saves the trajectory on context exhaustion without prompting. Harbor can then verify the existing patch.

Sotopia uses the packaged agent from merged [Harbor #231](https://github.com/marin-community/harbor/pull/231). Judge failures become verifier infrastructure errors. The Marin agent wrappers and their harness dependencies are removed. Sotopia's native generation still does not enforce its declared context budget, so those results cannot establish conformance to the 32K context policy.

Part of #9566.

topics.title: [grug] Correct hero remat and collective scheduling; build PGLE profiles
topics.body:
Carry-offloaded hero runs stop recomputing ~10 GiB of backward values per step that already fit in HBM, which shortens the step by 1.18% (13.899 to 13.737 s on one 64-GPU hero rack, restore step-180000, seed 0, 100 steps). Ragged runs without the carry offload run their collectives one at a time, and `pgle_profile` builds an XLA PGLE profile from one trace of the train step. No model code changes.

With the layer carry offloaded to pinned host memory, XLA's `HloRematerialization` charged the 36 GiB carry stack against the device memory limit and recomputed values that fit (143 remat clones, 0.63 s/step of compute). The launcher now defaults `--xla_gpu_enable_host_memory_offloading=true` whenever the carry is offloaded, so remat counts host buffers as host memory. Only the remat pass reads the flag, after scheduling and copy insertion, so it cannot reorder the carry reload against its consumer. XLA has no narrower flag: this one also lets remat offload values to host when device memory runs short, which a step that fits in HBM does not trigger.

A ragged run without the carry offload keeps the latency-hiding scheduler off, and the collective overlap limit binds only that scheduler, so XLA's default scheduler can start two ragged transports at once. Compiled for a mocked EP64 topology, the program does so in the forward and in the backward, and on GB200 several collectives in flight have hung the ragged transport or given run-to-run different gradients. The launcher now forces `--xla_gpu_disable_async_collectives=ALLCOLLECTIVES` for that configuration.

XLA's default latency estimator gives every collective the same small latency, so with one collective in flight it treats a multi-millisecond ragged transport as hidden under one GEMM. A profile built by `pgle_profile` from the program's own trace shortened the hero step with all of #9708 from 12.611 to 12.515 s (+0.77%). A profile applies only to the program it was traced from, so nothing uses one by default; the README describes the trace, build and rerun loop.

Split from #9708. Part of #9636.

topics.title: [grug] Keep AdamH updates finite on zero-norm matrices
topics.body:
scale_by_adamh projects onto the parameter's Frobenius sphere by dividing by
the updated matrix norm. A zero matrix stays zero through a zero learning-rate
or zero-gradient step, so the division is 0/0 and the update is NaN. Floor
that norm at 1e-10, the same floor the direction step already uses.

Fixes #9054

topics.title: [grug] Benchmark the June Snowball trainer on synthetic tokens
topics.body:
`experiments/june_tpu_67b_a2b/moe/synthetic_benchmark.py` runs the June 67B-A2B recipe's own trainer and model on synthetic tokens from one Slurm node, with no Fray or Iris, so the Grug code path can be measured on AMD GPUs (#9462) against Levanter's `SnowballConfig`. It builds the production model through the recipe's width heuristic with the cooldown launch's switches, feeds fresh uniform-random examples through `LmDataConfig` with a mixture block the length of the dataset so nothing repeats and the loss stays a leak check, and takes the same flags as the Snowball harness: presets, steps, batch, expert axis, mixed-precision policy, attention and MoE implementation, and a profile window.

The June trainer always created a checkpointer and force-saved the final state, about 1 TB for the 67B model. `GrugTrainerConfig` gains `save_checkpoints`; False skips the checkpointer entirely.

Measured on the AMD HPC Fund cluster at the full 67B shape on 8 GPUs, one 4096-token sequence per GPU, bf16 or fp16 compute with f32 params: MI350X bf16 FSDP 9.57 s per step (0.29% MFU), MI350X fp16 expert-parallel 1.09 s (2.59%), MI350X bf16 expert-parallel with the Triton `ragged_dot` 0.73 s (3.86%), MI300X bf16 FSDP 2.27 s (2.19%), MI300X bf16 expert-parallel about 0.76 s (6.5%). These agree with Levanter's `SnowballConfig` through the #9613 harness within about 10%. Details are in the baseline comment on #9462.

Part of #9462

topics.title: [fast-track] Marin Belay v1: hill-climb the scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss, 8 min on 8×H100)
topics.body:
This issue tracks iterative improvements to the Marin pretraining scaling ladder (`experiments/grug/fast_track`) using the **Marin Belay** process. It is a twist on autoresearch: an agent runs experiments in batches, and anyone can steer it with research directions. > **To suggest a research direction, comment on [Marin Belay Intake (#9514)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9514).** Suggestions a maintainer approves (👍 from a `marin-devs` member) are copied into this thread automatically, and the agent acts only on this thread. This thread holds the agent's batch reports and maintainer steering. ![fast_track MoE ladder: Marin 535B baseline, clean KMA and candidate 9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/marin-community/marin/9697c11ef215ec0f9d536a1bceb0876f768fcf26/v1/ladder_scaling.png) The Marin 535B compute-optimal baseline follows `L(C) = 1.2 + 59.0·C^(−0.0843)` over four data-matched rungs. Clean KMA, the current baseline (★), is 0.022 lower at d512, 0.049 lower at d768, 0.040 lower at d1024 and 0.033 lower at d1280, which is about 1.14×, 1.43×, 1.40× and 1.35× the baseline's compute efficiency. Its dashed curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 64.8·C^(−0.0870)`. The **?** marks the open question this issue is chasing: how much further down each point can go. The red diamonds are the current best recipe, candidate 9 (Status below): **2.977 / 2.725 / 2.515 / 2.397** at d512 / d768 / d1024 / d1280. d512 and d768 are seed means, and the bigram table follows rule A. d768–d1280 are data-matched; d512 sits at its fixed-time step count (2817 vs 2383 steps), so it's plotted slightly to the right. That is 0.157 / 0.098 / 0.078 / 0.074 below clean KMA. Its dash-dot curve is fit to all four points: `L(C) = 1.2 + 55.0·C^(−0.0847)`. Its slope is a little shallower than clean KMA's, so the gap narrows with compute: projected to **1e24 FLOPs, 1.710 vs clean KMA's 1.727, about 1.48× clean KMA's compute efficiency and 2.95× the 535B baseline's**. Because the fixed-time d512 point flattens the fitted slope, that projection is probably conservative. The right panel is clean KMA's training MFU at each rung on one 8×H100 node: 9.5% at d512 and d768, 12.2% at d1024, and 13.0% at d1280. FLOPs are counted from KMA's own layers (KDA, MLA + Inkling, AttnRes), as 3× forward with no recompute. The trainer's logged `throughput/mfu` uses the baseline architecture's FLOP formula, so it is slightly off for KMA. ## Objective **Minimize Paloma macro loss (`eval/paloma/macro_loss`, final step) at the d512 rung after a fixed 8 minutes of 8×H100 train-step time.** - **Fixed time, not fixed tokens.** Faster code trains on more tokens within the 8 minutes, so a pure speedup counts as a win. - The LR schedule depends on the step count, so fix steps before each run: `num_steps = round(480 s × ex/s ÷ batch)`. - Measure ex/s with a short `--no-eval` probe (~30 steps) on the same cluster, and use the steady-state throughput. - Compile, evals and startup are excluded from the 8 minutes. - **Numerics changes are allowed** (e.g. FP8, precision changes, approximate kernels). They count as ordinary wins; no parity check needed. - **Noise.** Differences under ~0.005 are noise. A win must beat the current best by more than 0.005. ### Gates (both relative to the current baseline, same fixed-time rule at each rung) - **Gate 1:** beat the baseline at d512 and d768. - **Gate 2:** also beat it at d1024 and d1280, **and** project to lower Paloma macro loss at 1e24 FLOPs. Fit a power law of final loss against training FLOPs across the four rungs, for both the baseline and the variant, fixing the asymptote to 1.2. ### Fixed - Training data, the 16k BPE tokenizer, and the eval sets. - Sequence length 4096. - One 8×H100 node per rung. - The FLOP accounting used for the gate-2 projection. ### Judgment calls - **Hero-scale speed is out of scope for v1, so use discretion.** - Robust target criteria would also check training speed and inference speed at hero scale. Marin Belay v1 skips those checks. - Judge whether a change's d512 gain would carry over to hero scale, and avoid changes whose gain comes from d512-only effects. Two examples: - Dropping MoE for dense would be a clear win at d512 because dense gets ~5× higher MFU there, but that MFU gain would not carry over at hero scale. - A much larger KV cache would also be a clear win at d512, but it would hurt long-context inference speed. - **Avoid magic numbers.** - Prefer changes with few new tuned constants. A tuned constant is justified when its gain is above the noise threshold and holds as a pattern across scales. For example, a 2× LR on one parameter group qualifies if it clears the noise threshold and the gain shows up consistently at larger rungs. - The higher a change's risk of curve fitting, the more scales it must be validated at before it counts as a win. - **Spend effort in proportion to an idea's likelihood of improvement.** - Promising ideas deserve several attempts. Long shots can be tried once and dropped. - A first run is not a verdict for a large change. If you try a new architecture or component, tune its optimizer assignment, LR, init and other key hyperparameters before concluding it doesn't work. The baseline's settings were tuned for the baseline, not for the new idea. ## Architecture (current best, d512) The diagrams below show **clean KMA**. The current best recipe adds the components listed under **Status → Current best recipe**: MLA key norm and key offset, a gated bigram-memory AttnRes source, ReLU² experts, and optimizer, schedule and logit changes. The diagrams show d512; the other rungs differ in the Shape table only. **1. Layer stack and Block Attention Residuals.** Every sublayer reads its input through its own AttnRes gate, a per-token softmax over the residual history. At d512 each layer closes an AttnRes block, so the history at layer *i* is the embedding plus one sum per earlier layer. [¹](#arch-note) ```mermaid flowchart TB tok["token ids

fused CE, vocab tile 8192, z-loss 1e-4"] head --> loss(["next-token loss"]) ``` **2. One layer.** The two sublayers each have an AttnRes gate. The MoE gate also sees the attention output written just before it, as the running partial. ```mermaid flowchart TB Hin[("history
